title: Esther

stories.title: 👑 Esther 1
summaryBullets: This is what happened in the days of Xerxes, who reigned over 127 provinces from India to Cush. (1:1).
In those days King Xerxes sat on his royal throne in the citadel of Susa. (1:2).
In the third year of his reign, Xerxes held a feast for all his officials and servants. The military leaders of Persia and Media were there, along with the nobles and princes of the provinces. (1:3).
And for a full 180 days he displayed the glorious riches of his kingdom and the magnificent splendor of his greatness. (1:4).
At the end of this time, in the garden court of the royal palace, the king held a seven-day feast for all the people in the citadel of Susa, from the least to the greatest. (1:5).

Hangings of white and blue linen were fastened with cords of fine white and purple material to silver rings on the marble pillars. Gold and silver couches were arranged on a mosaic pavement of porphyry, marble, mother-of-pearl, and other costly stones. (1:6).
Beverages were served in an array of goblets of gold, each with a different design, and the royal wine flowed freely, according to the king’s bounty. (1:7).
By order of the king, no limit was placed on the drinking, and every official of his household was to serve each man whatever he desired. (1:8).
Queen Vashti also gave a banquet for the women in the royal palace of King Xerxes. (1:9).
On the seventh day, when the king’s heart was merry with wine, he ordered the seven eunuchs who served him — Mehuman, Biztha, Harbona, Bigtha, Abagtha, Zethar, and Carkas — (1:10).
to bring Queen Vashti before him, wearing her royal crown, to display her beauty to the people and officials. For she was beautiful to behold. (1:11).
Queen Vashti, however, refused to come at the king’s command brought by his eunuchs. And the king became furious, and his anger burned within him. (1:12).
Then the king consulted the wise men who knew the times, for it was customary for him to confer with the experts in law and justice. (1:13).

His closest advisors were Carshena, Shethar, Admatha, Tarshish, Meres, Marsena, and Memucan, the seven princes of Persia and Media who had personal access to the king and ranked highest in the kingdom. (1:14).
“According to law,” he asked, “what should be done with Queen Vashti, since she refused to obey the command of King Xerxes delivered by the eunuchs?” (1:15).
And in the presence of the king and his princes, Memucan replied, “Queen Vashti has wronged not only the king, but all the princes and the peoples in all the provinces of King Xerxes. (1:16).
For the conduct of the queen will become known to all women, causing them to despise their husbands and say, ‘King Xerxes ordered Queen Vashti to be brought before him, but she did not come.’ (1:17).
This very day the noble women of Persia and Media who have heard about the queen’s conduct will say the same thing to all the king’s officials, resulting in much contempt and wrath. (1:18).

So if it pleases the king, let him issue a royal decree, and let it be recorded in the laws of Persia and Media so that it cannot be repealed, that Vashti shall never again enter the presence of King Xerxes, and that her royal position shall be given to a woman better than she. (1:19).
The edict the king issues will be heard throughout his vast kingdom — and so all women, from the least to the greatest, will honor their husbands.” (1:20).
The king and his princes were pleased with this counsel; so the king did as Memucan advised. (1:21).

He sent letters to all the provinces of the kingdom, to each province in its own script and to each people in their own language, proclaiming that every man should be master of his own household. (1:22).
crossRefs: Ezra 4:6: At the beginning of the reign of Ahasuerus, an accusation against the people of Judah is written to this same king.
Nehemiah 1:1-2: Nehemiah is serving in Susa the citadel, the same royal residence, about thirty-five years later.
Daniel 5:1-4: A king holds a great feast for his nobles, drinks with them, and sends for the sacred vessels.
Daniel 6:6-9: A Persian decree, once signed, cannot be altered under the law of the Medes and Persians.
1 Kings 10:18-21: Solomon's throne of ivory and gold, and drinking vessels of gold because silver counted for nothing.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֲחַשְׁוֵרוֹשׁ (Achashverosh) - Old Persian: Khshayarsha - Greek: Ξέρξης (Xerxes)
translationNotes.note: The Hebrew spells the Persian throne name Khshayarsha directly; Greek writers rendered the same name as Xerxes, which is why English Bibles sometimes print one and sometimes the other. Xerxes I reigned 486 to 465 BC, so the third year in 1:3 falls in 483 BC and the seventh year in 2:16 in 479 BC. The six months of display in this chapter fall in the years he was assembling the invasion of Greece.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מְדִינָה (medinah, province or administrative district)
translationNotes.note: A medinah is not a satrapy. Herodotus (Histories 3.89) says Darius organised the empire into twenty satrapies for tribute, and the provinces were the smaller districts inside them, each with its own governor, script and language. From India, the Indus country, to Cush, the land south of Egypt, is some three thousand miles, and 1:1 is giving the width of the empire, not a count of nations.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שׁוּשַׁן הַבִּירָה (Shushan habbirah)
translationNotes.note: Birah means the walled palace acropolis, raised above the city and separate from it, which is why the text keeps distinguishing 'Susa the citadel' from 'the city of Susa' (3:15; 8:14-15; 9:6, 12-15). Susa lies in Khuzestan in southwestern Iran, in hot lowland country, and the Persian court wintered there. French excavations from 1884 uncovered the palace of Darius, its great columned audience hall, and a monumental gatehouse carrying an inscription of Xerxes.

translationNotes.term: The drinking was by law, without compulsion
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: וְהַשְּׁתִיָּה כַדָּת אֵין אֹנֵס (vehashshetiyyah khaddat ein ones)
translationNotes.note: At a Persian banquet the guests drank when the king drank and matched him. Verse 8 records that this rule was suspended and each man could drink as he pleased, which is the detail the text bothers to mention. Herodotus (Histories 1.133) writes that the Persians deliberated important matters over wine and reviewed the decision sober, so what a king decides at the end of a seven-day feast is not a footnote.

translationNotes.term: The seven who saw the king's face
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: רֹאֵי פְּנֵי הַמֶּלֶךְ (ro'ei penei hammelekh, seers of the king's face)
translationNotes.note: Verse 14 names seven princes of Persia and Media who saw the king's face and sat first in the kingdom. Access to the king's presence was the currency of that court; Herodotus (3.84) reports that the seven Persian nobles who put Darius on the throne kept the standing right to enter unannounced. Seven eunuchs are named in the same chapter as the servants of the inner rooms.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חוּר כַּרְפַּס וּתְכֵלֶת (chur karpas u-tekhelet, white cotton and violet)
translationNotes.note: Verse 6 is an inventory: white and violet hangings tied with cords of fine linen and purple to silver rings on marble pillars, couches of gold and silver standing on a pavement of porphyry, marble, mother-of-pearl and coloured stone. Tekhelet, the violet-blue, and purple were the two dyes drawn from murex shellfish and were the most expensive colours in the ancient world. The list is a valuation, and it is put at the front of the book on purpose.

stories.keyTakeaway: King Xerxes displays his wealth for 180 days, then holds a seven-day banquet where he orders Queen Vashti to appear before him; when she refuses, he consults his nobles and has her removed from her position by royal decree.

stories.title: 👑 Esther 2
summaryBullets: Some time later, when the anger of King Xerxes had subsided, he remembered Vashti and what she had done, and what had been decreed against her. (2:1).
Then the king’s attendants proposed, “Let a search be made for beautiful young virgins for the king, (2:2).

and let the king appoint commissioners in each province of his kingdom to assemble all the beautiful young women into the harem at the citadel of Susa. Let them be placed under the care of Hegai, the king’s eunuch in charge of the women, and let them be given beauty treatments. (2:3).
Then let the young woman who pleases the king become queen in place of Vashti.” This suggestion pleased the king, and he acted accordingly. (2:4).
Now there was at the citadel of Susa a Jewish man from the tribe of Benjamin named Mordecai son of Jair, the son of Shimei, the son of Kish. (2:5).
He had been carried into exile from Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon among those taken captive with Jeconiah king of Judah. (2:6).

And Mordecai had brought up Hadassah (that is, Esther), the daughter of his uncle, because she did not have a father or mother. The young woman was lovely in form and appearance, and when her father and mother had died, Mordecai had taken her as his own daughter. (2:7).

When the king’s command and edict had been proclaimed, many young women gathered at the citadel of Susa under the care of Hegai. Esther was also taken to the palace and placed under the care of Hegai, the custodian of the women. (2:8).

And the young woman pleased him and obtained his favor, so he quickly provided her with beauty treatments and the special diet. He assigned to her seven select maidservants from the palace and transferred her with them to the best place in the harem. (2:9).
Esther did not reveal her people or her lineage, because Mordecai had instructed her not to do so. (2:10).
And every day Mordecai would walk back and forth in front of the court of the harem to learn about Esther’s welfare and what was happening to her. (2:11).

In the twelve months before her turn to go to King Xerxes, the harem regulation required each young woman to receive beauty treatments with oil of myrrh for six months, and then with perfumes and cosmetics for another six months. (2:12).
When the young woman would go to the king, she was given whatever she requested to take with her from the harem to the king’s palace. (2:13).

She would go there in the evening, and in the morning she would return to a second harem under the care of Shaashgaz, the king’s eunuch in charge of the concubines. She would not return to the king unless he delighted in her and summoned her by name. (2:14).

Now Esther was the daughter of Abihail, the uncle from whom Mordecai had adopted her as his own daughter. And when it was her turn to go to the king, she did not ask for anything except what Hegai, the king’s trusted official in charge of the harem, had advised. And Esther found favor in the eyes of everyone who saw her. (2:15).
She was taken to King Xerxes in the royal palace in the tenth month, the month of Tebeth, in the seventh year of his reign. (2:16).

And the king loved Esther more than all the other women, and she found grace and favor in his sight more than all of the other virgins. So he placed the royal crown upon her head and made her queen in place of Vashti. (2:17).
Then the king held a great banquet, Esther’s banquet, for all his officials and servants. He proclaimed a tax holiday in the provinces and gave gifts worthy of the king’s bounty. (2:18).
When the virgins were assembled a second time, Mordecai was sitting at the king’s gate. (2:19).
Esther still had not revealed her lineage or her people, just as Mordecai had instructed. She obeyed Mordecai’s command, as she had done under his care. (2:20).
In those days, while Mordecai was sitting at the king’s gate, Bigthan and Teresh, two of the king’s eunuchs who guarded the entrance, grew angry and conspired to assassinate King Xerxes. (2:21).
When Mordecai learned of the plot, he reported it to Queen Esther, and she informed the king on Mordecai’s behalf. (2:22).
After the report had been investigated and verified, both officials were hanged on the gallows. And all this was recorded in the Book of the Chronicles in the presence of the king. (2:23).
crossRefs: Genesis 41:37-45: A Hebrew is raised over a foreign court, given a new name, a signet ring and fine clothing.
Daniel 1:3-7: Young Judeans are taken into the palace, trained for the king's service, and given Babylonian names.
2 Kings 24:12-16: Jeconiah king of Judah and the people of Jerusalem are carried away to Babylon, the exile this family came out of.
1 Samuel 8:11-18: Samuel warns that a king will take your sons and your daughters and your fields for himself.
Esther 6:1-3: Years later the record of this assassination plot is read aloud to a sleepless king.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הֲדַסָּה (Hadassah, myrtle) - אֶסְתֵּר (Ester)
translationNotes.note: Verse 7 gives both names: Hadassah is Hebrew for the myrtle, an evergreen shrub used for the branches of the Feast of Booths (Nehemiah 8:15). Esther matches the Persian word for star, stara. Judeans in imperial service commonly carried two names, one for home and one for the court, as Daniel and his three friends did.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: סָרִיס (saris) - Greek: εὐνοῦχος (eunouchos)
translationNotes.note: Castrated men staffed the royal household because they could be trusted around the king's women and could found no dynasty of their own. Hegai keeps the virgins and Shaashgaz keeps the concubines (2:3, 14); seven more are named as the king's personal attendants (1:10). The same Hebrew word is used more loosely elsewhere for a court officer, as with Potiphar, who was married (Genesis 39:1).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שִׁשָּׁה חֳדָשִׁים בְּשֶׁמֶן הַמֹּר (shishah chodashim beshemen hammor, six months with oil of myrrh)
translationNotes.note: Verse 12 sets out the regimen: six months with oil of myrrh, then six months with spices and cosmetics, before a woman went in to the king once. Whatever she asked for went with her, and in the morning she passed to the second house under a different keeper and did not go back unless the king summoned her by name (2:13-14). This is the machinery of a royal harem stated flatly, without comment.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מֹר (mor) - Greek: σμύρνα (smyrna)
translationNotes.note: A gum resin bled from the bark of the Commiphora tree in Arabia and East Africa, imported by caravan and expensive. It was an ingredient of the holy anointing oil (Exodus 30:23), a perfume, a burial spice (John 19:39) and, mixed with wine, a pain-dulling drink (Mark 15:23). Six months of daily treatment with it is a statement of what the crown could spend.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שַׁעַר הַמֶּלֶךְ (sha'ar hammelekh)
translationNotes.note: Not a doorway but the monumental gatehouse of the palace complex, where officials sat on duty and business was transacted. Excavation at Susa uncovered such a gatehouse, a square hall about forty metres on a side, with an inscription of Xerxes recording that Darius his father built it. When 2:19 and 2:21 say Mordecai was sitting in the king's gate, they are telling you he held a post there.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הָגְלָה עִם־יְכָנְיָה (hoglah im Yekhonyah)
translationNotes.note: Verse 6 traces the family to the deportation of Jeconiah king of Judah, which took place in 597 BC (2 Kings 24:12-16), more than a hundred years before the events of this book. Mordecai is a Benjaminite descended from Kish (2:5), the name of the father of King Saul. That descent is what makes the collision with an Agagite in the next chapter a very old quarrel.

stories.keyTakeaway: King Xerxes searches for a new queen and selects Esther, a Jewish orphan raised by her cousin Mordecai, who becomes queen after winning the king's favor. Mordecai later uncovers an assassination plot against the king and reports it through Esther, saving the king's life.

stories.title: 🎲 Esther 3
summaryBullets: After these events, King Xerxes honored Haman son of Hammedatha, the Agagite, elevating him to a position above all the princes who were with him. (3:1).
All the royal servants at the king’s gate bowed down and paid homage to Haman, because the king had commanded that this be done for him. But Mordecai would not bow down or pay homage. (3:2).
Then the royal servants at the king’s gate asked Mordecai, “Why do you disobey the command of the king?” (3:3).
Day after day they warned him, but he would not comply. So they reported it to Haman to see whether Mordecai’s behavior would be tolerated, since he had told them he was a Jew. (3:4).
When Haman saw that Mordecai would not bow down or pay him homage, he was filled with rage. (3:5).

And when he learned the identity of Mordecai’s people, he scorned the notion of laying hands on Mordecai alone. Instead, he sought to destroy all of Mordecai’s people, the Jews, throughout the kingdom of Xerxes. (3:6).

In the twelfth year of King Xerxes, in the first month, the month of Nisan, the Pur (that is, the lot) was cast before Haman to determine a day and month. And the lot fell on the twelfth month, the month of Adar. (3:7).

Then Haman informed King Xerxes, “There is a certain people scattered and dispersed among the peoples of every province of your kingdom. Their laws are different from everyone else’s, and they do not obey the king’s laws. So it is not in the king’s best interest to tolerate them. (3:8).
If it pleases the king, let a decree be issued to destroy them, and I will deposit ten thousand talents of silver into the royal treasury to pay those who carry it out.” (3:9).
So the king removed the signet ring from his finger and gave it to Haman son of Hammedatha, the Agagite, the enemy of the Jews. (3:10).
“Keep your money,” said the king to Haman. “These people are given to you to do with them as you please.” (3:11).

On the thirteenth day of the first month, the royal scribes were summoned and the order was written exactly as Haman commanded the royal satraps, the governors of each province, and the officials of each people, in the script of each province and the language of every people. It was written in the name of King Xerxes and sealed with the royal signet ring. (3:12).

And the letters were sent by couriers to each of the royal provinces with the order to destroy, kill, and annihilate all the Jews— young and old, women and children— and to plunder their possessions on a single day, the thirteenth day of Adar, the twelfth month. (3:13).
A copy of the text of the edict was to be issued in every province and published to all the people, so that they would be ready on that day. (3:14).
The couriers left, spurred on by the king’s command, and the edict was issued in the citadel of Susa. Then the king and Haman sat down to drink, but the city of Susa was in confusion. (3:15).
crossRefs: Exodus 17:8-13: Amalek attacks Israel at Rephidim, and Israel prevails only while Moses' hands are held up.
Deuteronomy 25:17-19: Remember what Amalek did to you on the way out of Egypt, and blot out the memory of Amalek.
1 Samuel 15:1-9: Saul defeats Amalek but spares Agag their king and the best of the livestock.
1 Samuel 9:1-2: Kish the Benjaminite, father of Saul, the family line Mordecai is traced from.
Proverbs 16:33: The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision comes from the LORD.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הָאֲגָגִי (ha-Agagi)
translationNotes.note: Agag was the king of Amalek whom Saul spared against the command, and whom Samuel then executed (1 Samuel 15:8-9, 32-33). Amalek had attacked Israel at Rephidim on the way out of Egypt, and Exodus 17:16 and Deuteronomy 25:17-19 record a standing war with them. Haman is labelled with that people; Mordecai is traced to Kish the Benjaminite, Saul's own family. The book sets those two lines against each other without saying another word about it.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: פּוּר (pur) - Akkadian: puru - Hebrew gloss: גּוֹרָל (goral, lot)
translationNotes.note: The text stops to translate the word for its readers: 'they cast pur, that is, the lot' (3:7). Pur is Akkadian, not Hebrew, and the object is a small inscribed die. One survives: a clay cube about an inch across, naming Yahali, chief steward of Shalmaneser III, cast to decide the year that fell to him, 833 BC. Haman casts lots in the first month to fix a date in the twelfth, which leaves eleven months on the clock.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עֲשֶׂרֶת אֲלָפִים כִּכַּר־כֶּסֶף (aseret alafim kikkar kesef)
translationNotes.note: A talent weighed about 75 pounds, so Haman is offering roughly 340 metric tons, 375 tons, of silver into the royal treasury. Herodotus (Histories 3.95) puts the entire annual tribute of the Persian empire at 14,560 talents. The offer runs to about two thirds of a year's imperial revenue, and the king waves it away.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֲחַשְׁדַּרְפְּנִים (achashdarpenim) - from Old Persian khshathrapavan, protector of the realm
translationNotes.note: Verse 12 lists three ranks in descending order: satraps over the great regions, governors over each province, and the princes of each people. The Hebrew word for satrap is a straight loan from Old Persian, as is the word for the royal law, dat. The book uses the empire's own vocabulary for the empire's own machinery.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: רָצִים (ratsim, runners)
translationNotes.note: The edict is written in every province's script and language, sealed with the king's ring, and handed to the couriers (3:12-15). Herodotus (8.98) describes the Persian relay: riders and horses posted a day's ride apart, each handing off to the next, so that nothing mortal travels faster. The road from Susa to Sardis ran a hundred and eleven posting stations and about fifteen hundred miles (Herodotus 5.52-53). This is how one decision in the citadel reaches India inside a month.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֲדָר (Adar)
translationNotes.note: Adar is the twelfth month, mid-February to mid-March, the last month before the spring new year. The lot fell in Nisan, the first month, for a date eleven months out, so every Jew in the empire had nearly a year to read the notice and wait. Verse 15 ends with the couriers going out in haste, the king and Haman sitting down to drink, and the city of Susa thrown into confusion.

stories.keyTakeaway: King Xerxes elevates Haman above all nobles; when Mordecai refuses to kneel to him, Haman plots to destroy all the Jews throughout the kingdom. The king approves the plan and issues an edict ordering the extermination of every Jew on the thirteenth day of Adar.

stories.title: 🎲 Esther 4
summaryBullets: When Mordecai learned of all that had happened, he tore his clothes, put on sackcloth and ashes, and went out into the middle of the city, wailing loudly and bitterly. (4:1).
But he went only as far as the king’s gate, because the law prohibited anyone wearing sackcloth from entering that gate. (4:2).
In every province to which the king’s command and edict came, there was great mourning among the Jews. They fasted, wept, and lamented, and many lay in sackcloth and ashes. (4:3).

When Esther’s maidens and eunuchs came and told her about Mordecai, the queen was overcome with distress. She sent clothes for Mordecai to wear instead of his sackcloth, but he would not accept them. (4:4).
Then Esther summoned Hathach, one of the king’s eunuchs appointed to her, and she dispatched him to Mordecai to learn what was troubling him and why. (4:5).
So Hathach went out to Mordecai in the city square in front of the king’s gate, (4:6).
and Mordecai told him all that had happened to him, including the exact amount of money that Haman had promised to pay into the royal treasury in order to destroy the Jews. (4:7).

Mordecai also gave Hathach a copy of the written decree issued in Susa for the destruction of the Jews, to show and explain to Esther, urging her to approach the king, implore his favor, and plead before him for her people. (4:8).
So Hathach went back and relayed Mordecai’s response to Esther. (4:9).
Then Esther spoke to Hathach and instructed him to tell Mordecai, (4:10).

“All the royal officials and the people of the king’s provinces know that one law applies to every man or woman who approaches the king in the inner court without being summoned— that he be put to death. Only if the king extends the gold scepter may that person live. But I have not been summoned to appear before the king for the past thirty days.” (4:11).
When Esther’s words were relayed to Mordecai, (4:12).
he sent back to her this reply: “Do not imagine that because you are in the king’s palace you alone will escape the fate of all the Jews. (4:13).

For if you remain silent at this time, relief and deliverance for the Jews will arise from another place, but you and your father’s house will perish. And who knows if perhaps you have come to the kingdom for such a time as this?” (4:14).
Then Esther sent this reply to Mordecai: (4:15).

“Go and assemble all the Jews who can be found in Susa, and fast for me. Do not eat or drink for three days, night or day, and I and my maidens will fast as you do. After that, I will go to the king, even though it is against the law. And if I perish, I perish!” (4:16).
So Mordecai went and did all that Esther had instructed him. (4:17).
crossRefs: Joel 2:12-17: Return with fasting, weeping and mourning; call a solemn assembly and gather the people.
Jonah 3:5-9: Nineveh proclaims a fast and puts on sackcloth from the greatest of them to the least.
Ezra 8:21-23: Ezra proclaims a fast at the river Ahava to seek a safe journey, rather than ask the king for troops.
Daniel 3:16-18: Three men refuse the image, saying God is able to deliver them, and that even if He does not, they will not serve it.
Genesis 45:4-8: Joseph tells his brothers that God sent him ahead of them to preserve a remnant alive.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שַׂק וָאֵפֶר (saq va-efer)
translationNotes.note: Sackcloth is coarse dark goat-hair cloth worn against bare skin, deliberately uncomfortable, the standard public sign of grief or repentance (1 Kings 21:27; Jonah 3:5). Mordecai wears it into the middle of the city with a loud and bitter cry (4:1), and 4:2 gives the rule that stops him at the gate: no one may enter the king's gate dressed in sackcloth. Grief was not permitted inside the palace.

translationNotes.term: The law of the inner court
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אַחַת דָּתוֹ לְהָמִית (achat dato lehamit, there is one law for him, to be put to death)
translationNotes.note: Anyone who goes into the inner court to the king without being called is put to death, unless the king holds out the golden sceptre (4:11). Esther adds that she has not been summoned for thirty days. Herodotus (3.118-119) reports a Persian noble who was refused admission to Darius, mutilated the doorkeepers, and was executed with most of his family. Access to the king was policed with lethal seriousness.

translationNotes.term: Neither eat nor drink for three days
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אַל־תֹּאכְלוּ וְאַל־תִּשְׁתּוּ שְׁלֹשֶׁת יָמִים לַיְלָה וָיוֹם (al tokhelu ve-al tishtu sheloshet yamim laylah va-yom)
translationNotes.note: Fasts in Scripture normally run from morning to evening (Judges 20:26; 2 Samuel 1:12). What Esther calls for in 4:16 is total, no food and no water, night and day, for three days, by every Jew in Susa. Going without water for three days in that climate is dangerous in itself. The book never uses the word prayer here, and it never names God, but this is what the people do.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הֲתָךְ (Hathakh)
translationNotes.note: The queen could not walk out to the city square, and Mordecai could not come in past the gate in sackcloth, so the entire negotiation of chapter 4 runs through a eunuch carrying messages back and forth across a wall (4:5-12). Mordecai even hands him a written copy of the decree to show her. The most consequential conversation in the book is conducted by relay.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: רֶוַח וְהַצָּלָה יַעֲמוֹד לַיְּהוּדִים מִמָּקוֹם אַחֵר (revach vehatsalah ya'amod layehudim mimmaqom acher)
translationNotes.note: Mordecai's argument in 4:13-14 has three parts: she will not escape by being in the palace, deliverance will arise from somewhere else if she keeps silent, and who knows whether she has come to the kingdom for a time like this. He does not name who or what the other place is. The text leaves the sentence exactly as he said it.

stories.keyTakeaway: Mordecai learns of the edict to destroy the Jews and, after grieving in sackcloth, sends word to Esther urging her to petition the king; Esther initially refuses, citing the danger, but Mordecai warns her that silence will not save her, and she agrees to fast and approach the king despite the law forbidding it.

stories.title: 🍷 Esther 5
summaryBullets: On the third day, Esther put on her royal robes and stood in the inner court of the palace across from the king’s quarters. The king was sitting on his royal throne in the royal courtroom, facing the entrance. (5:1).

As soon as the king saw Queen Esther standing in the court, she found favor in his sight. The king extended the gold scepter in his hand toward Esther, and she approached and touched the tip of the scepter. (5:2).
“What is it, Queen Esther?” the king inquired. “What is your request? Even up to half the kingdom, it will be given to you.” (5:3).
“If it pleases the king,” Esther replied, “may the king and Haman come today to the banquet I have prepared for the king.” (5:4).
“Hurry,” commanded the king, “and bring Haman, so we can do as Esther has requested.” So the king and Haman went to the banquet that Esther had prepared. (5:5).
And as they drank their wine, the king said to Esther, “What is your petition? It will be given to you. What is your request? Even up to half the kingdom, it will be fulfilled.” (5:6).
Esther replied, “This is my petition and my request: (5:7).

If I have found favor in the sight of the king, and if it pleases the king to grant my petition and fulfill my request, may the king and Haman come tomorrow to the banquet I will prepare for them. Then I will answer the king’s question.” (5:8).

That day Haman went out full of joy and glad of heart. At the king’s gate, however, he saw Mordecai, who did not rise or tremble in fear at his presence. And Haman was filled with rage toward Mordecai. (5:9).
Nevertheless, Haman restrained himself and went home. And calling for his friends and his wife Zeresh, (5:10).
Haman recounted to them his glorious wealth, his many sons, and all the ways the king had honored and promoted him over the other officials and servants. (5:11).
“What is more,” Haman added, “Queen Esther invited no one but me to join the king at the banquet she prepared, and I am invited back tomorrow along with the king. (5:12).
Yet none of this satisfies me as long as I see Mordecai the Jew sitting at the king’s gate.” (5:13).

His wife Zeresh and all his friends told him, “Have them build a gallows fifty cubits high, and ask the king in the morning to have Mordecai hanged on it. Then go to the banquet with the king and enjoy yourself.” The advice pleased Haman, and he had the gallows constructed. (5:14).
crossRefs: Proverbs 16:14-15: A king's wrath is a messenger of death, but in the light of a king's face there is life.
1 Kings 2:19-20: Bathsheba comes to King Solomon, who rises to meet her, seats her at his right hand, and tells her to make her request.
Mark 6:21-23: Herod swears to a girl at his birthday feast that he will give her whatever she asks, up to half his kingdom.
Ecclesiastes 8:2-4: The king's word is supreme, and no one may ask him what he is doing.
Proverbs 25:6-7: Do not put yourself forward in the king's presence; better to be told, Come up here.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: וַתִּלְבַּשׁ אֶסְתֵּר מַלְכוּת (vattilbash Ester malkhut)
translationNotes.note: The Hebrew of 5:1 says she clothed herself in royalty, not in royal clothes; the word is the abstract noun for kingship. She takes her stand in the inner court facing the throne room, at the far end of the king's line of sight. The three days of fasting have just ended.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שַׁרְבִיט הַזָּהָב (sharvit hazzahav)
translationNotes.note: Persian reliefs from Persepolis show the enthroned king holding a long slender staff in his right hand, the height of a man. Extending it toward a petitioner cancelled the death sentence for approaching unbidden, and touching its tip was the acknowledgement (5:2). The gesture is the whole legal procedure, performed without a word.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עַד־חֲצִי הַמַּלְכוּת (ad chatsi hammalkhut)
translationNotes.note: A court formula of extravagant favour, offered three times in this book (5:3, 5:6, 7:2) and never meant as a literal partition of the empire. Herod uses the identical phrase in Mark 6:23. It signals that the petitioner may name a large request, and it commits the king in public.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מִשְׁתֵּה הַיַּיִן (mishteh hayyayin)
translationNotes.note: A Persian banquet ran in two stages: the food, then the drinking, where business was raised and decisions were made. Esther invites the king and Haman to the drinking on the first day, and then, instead of asking, invites them again for the next day (5:6-8). She lets the king go to bed with an unanswered question, and 6:1 records that he could not sleep.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עֵץ גָּבֹהַּ חֲמִשִּׁים אַמָּה (ets gavoah chamishshim ammah, wood fifty cubits high)
translationNotes.note: A cubit is about eighteen inches, so fifty cubits is roughly seventy-five feet, higher than any house in Susa, which is the point: it is meant to be seen from everywhere. The Hebrew word is ets, wood or tree, and the verb used with it means to hang or fasten upon. Persian executions of this kind were impalings, and Ezra 6:11 describes the same penalty in the same empire: a beam pulled from a man's house and the man fastened on it.

stories.keyTakeaway: Esther gains the king's favor and invites him and Haman to a banquet, deferring her request until a second banquet the next day. Haman leaves elated by his prominence but grows enraged seeing Mordecai unmoved at the gate; his wife and friends urge him to have Mordecai executed, and he orders a pole built for this purpose.

stories.title: 🍷 Esther 6
summaryBullets: That night sleep escaped the king; so he ordered the Book of Records, the Chronicles, to be brought in and read to him. (6:1).
And there it was found recorded that Mordecai had exposed Bigthana and Teresh, two of the eunuchs who guarded the king’s entrance, when they had conspired to assassinate King Xerxes. (6:2).
The king inquired, “What honor or dignity has been bestowed on Mordecai for this act?” “Nothing has been done for him,” replied the king’s attendants. (6:3).
“Who is in the court?” the king asked. Now Haman had just entered the outer court of the palace to ask the king to hang Mordecai on the gallows he had prepared for him. (6:4).
So the king’s attendants answered him, “Haman is there, standing in the court.” “Bring him in,” ordered the king. (6:5).

Haman entered, and the king asked him, “What should be done for the man whom the king is delighted to honor?” Now Haman thought to himself, “Whom would the king be delighted to honor more than me?” (6:6).
And Haman told the king, “For the man whom the king is delighted to honor, (6:7).
have them bring a royal robe that the king himself has worn and a horse on which the king himself has ridden— one with a royal crest placed on its head. (6:8).

Let the robe and the horse be entrusted to one of the king’s most noble princes. Let them array the man the king wants to honor and parade him on the horse through the city square, proclaiming before him, ‘This is what is done for the man whom the king is delighted to honor!’” (6:9).

“Hurry,” said the king to Haman, “and do just as you proposed. Take the robe and the horse to Mordecai the Jew, who is sitting at the king’s gate. Do not neglect anything that you have suggested.” (6:10).
So Haman took the robe and the horse, arrayed Mordecai, and paraded him through the city square, crying out before him, “This is what is done for the man whom the king is delighted to honor!” (6:11).
Then Mordecai returned to the king’s gate. But Haman rushed home, with his head covered in grief. (6:12).

Haman told his wife Zeresh and all his friends everything that had happened. His advisers and his wife Zeresh said to him, “Since Mordecai, before whom your downfall has begun, is Jewish, you will not prevail against him — for surely you will fall before him.” (6:13).
While they were still speaking with Haman, the king’s eunuchs arrived and rushed him to the banquet that Esther had prepared. (6:14).
crossRefs: 1 Samuel 18:3-4: Jonathan strips off the robe he is wearing and gives it to David, with his armour, sword, bow and belt.
1 Kings 1:32-40: Solomon is set on the king's own mule and led through the city with trumpets and shouting.
Ezra 6:1-5: A Persian king orders a search of the archives, and an old scroll is found that reverses a policy.
Esther 2:21-23: The plot against the king that Mordecai reported and that was written in the book of the chronicles.
Proverbs 26:27: Whoever digs a pit will fall into it, and a stone rolled uphill comes back on the one who rolled it.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: סֵפֶר הַזִּכְרֹנוֹת דִּבְרֵי הַיָּמִים (sefer hazzikhronot divrei hayyamim, the book of records, the matters of the days)
translationNotes.note: The Persian court kept a running written record of the reign, and it could be pulled and read aloud on demand. Ezra 4:15 and 6:1-2 show the same archive searched in the same period on a matter of Jewish policy. The turn of this whole book happens because a bureaucracy files things properly and a king cannot sleep.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: לְבוּשׁ מַלְכוּת וְסוּס אֲשֶׁר רָכַב עָלָיו הַמֶּלֶךְ (levush malkhut ve-sus asher rakhav alav hammelekh, royal clothing and a horse the king has ridden)
translationNotes.note: Haman's own proposal in 6:8-9 has three parts: a robe the king has worn, a horse the king has ridden, and a royal crown set on the horse's head, with one of the highest nobles leading the horse through the city square crying the proclamation. Wearing the king's clothes and riding his mount was to be marked as the king's own, which is exactly why Haman asks for it.

translationNotes.term: The man whom the king delights to honour
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הָאִישׁ אֲשֶׁר הַמֶּלֶךְ חָפֵץ בִּיקָרוֹ (ha-ish asher hammelekh chafets biqaro)
translationNotes.note: The phrase is repeated five times in six verses (6:6-11), a formal court formula being turned over and over. Haman hears it four times before he learns who it is about. The repetition is the joke, and it is built into the Hebrew.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: וְרֹאשׁ חָפוּי (ve-rosh chafuy, and his head covered)
translationNotes.note: Haman hurries home mourning with his head covered (6:12). Covering the head was a sign of grief and shame; David went up the Mount of Olives weeping with his head covered when he fled Absalom (2 Samuel 15:30). Mordecai, meanwhile, goes straight back to the king's gate, because he still has a job.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חֲכָמָיו וְזֶרֶשׁ אִשְׁתּוֹ (chakhamav ve-Zeresh ishto, his wise men and Zeresh his wife)
translationNotes.note: The same household council that told him to build the pole in 5:14 now tells him he has begun to fall and will not prevail (6:13). Wealthy Persian households kept advisers, and Haman convenes his twice in two chapters. Their reasoning is stated in the text as a fact about Mordecai's descent, and while they are still speaking the king's eunuchs arrive to bring him to the second banquet.

stories.keyTakeaway: Unable to sleep, King Xerxes learns that Mordecai once saved him from assassination and received no reward; he then orders Haman to honor Mordecai publicly with royal robes and a horse. Haman, who had intended to execute Mordecai, must carry out the honor himself, then rushes home in despair as his advisers warn him of his coming ruin.

stories.title: ⚖️ Esther 7
summaryBullets: So the king and Haman went to dine with Esther the queen, (7:1).

and as they drank their wine on that second day, the king asked once more, “Queen Esther, what is your petition? It will be given to you. What is your request? Even up to half the kingdom, it will be fulfilled.” (7:2).
Queen Esther replied, “If I have found favor in your sight, O king, and if it pleases the king, grant me my life as my petition, and the lives of my people as my request. (7:3).

For my people and I have been sold out to destruction, death, and annihilation. If we had merely been sold as menservants and maidservants, I would have remained silent, because no such distress would justify burdening the king.” (7:4).
Then King Xerxes spoke up and asked Queen Esther, “Who is this, and where is the one who would devise such a scheme?” (7:5).
Esther replied, “The adversary and enemy is this wicked man — Haman!” And Haman stood in terror before the king and queen. (7:6).

In his fury, the king arose from drinking his wine and went to the palace garden, while Haman stayed behind to beg Queen Esther for his life, for he realized that the king was planning a terrible fate for him. (7:7).

Just as the king returned from the palace garden to the banquet hall, Haman was falling on the couch where Esther was reclining. The king exclaimed, “Would he actually assault the queen while I am in the palace?” As soon as the words had left the king’s mouth, they covered Haman’s face. (7:8).

Then Harbonah, one of the eunuchs attending the king, said: “There is a gallows fifty cubits high at Haman’s house. He had it built for Mordecai, who gave the report that saved the king.” “Hang him on it!” declared the king. (7:9).
So they hanged Haman on the gallows he had prepared for Mordecai. Then the fury of the king subsided. (7:10).
crossRefs: Esther 5:9-14: Haman's wife and friends advise the pole, seventy-five feet high, and he has it built that night.
Ezra 6:11: In the same empire, whoever violates the decree has a beam pulled from his house and is fastened on it.
Genesis 40:19-22: Pharaoh's chief baker is hanged on a tree on the third day, exactly as Joseph read the dream.
Daniel 6:24: The men who accused Daniel are thrown into the den they arranged for him.
Psalm 7:14-16: The man who digs a pit falls into it, and his violence comes down on his own head.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נִמְכַּרְנוּ (nimkarnu, we have been sold)
translationNotes.note: Esther's phrasing in 7:4 picks up Haman's offer of ten thousand talents in 3:9: her people have literally been sold. She adds that if they had only been sold as slaves she would have kept quiet, because that loss would not have been worth troubling the king with. The word for destruction, killing and annihilation she uses is the exact wording of the edict in 3:13.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: לִכְבּוֹשׁ אֶת־הַמַּלְכָּה עִמִּי בַּבָּיִת (likhbosh et hammalkah immi babbayit, to force the queen while I am in the house)
translationNotes.note: Guests at a Persian banquet reclined on couches rather than sitting. When the king storms out to the garden and comes back, Haman has thrown himself onto the couch where Esther is lying, begging for his life (7:8). The king reads it as an assault on the queen in his own house, and the verb he uses means to subdue or force. Whether that was the intention or not, the sentence lands on the word.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: וּפְנֵי הָמָן חָפוּ (u-fenei Haman chafu)
translationNotes.note: As soon as the words left the king's mouth, attendants covered Haman's face (7:8). Veiling the head of a condemned man before execution was a known practice in the ancient world; Roman law preserved the old formula for it, caput obnubito, cover his head (Livy 1.26). The covering is the sentence being carried out, not an act of mercy.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חַרְבוֹנָה (Charvonah)
translationNotes.note: One of the seven eunuchs named back in 1:10 as attendants of the king's presence. It is he who mentions that a seventy-five foot pole is already standing at Haman's house, built for the man who spoke up and saved the king (7:9). Court servants knew what stood in the yards of the powerful, and he chose that moment to say so.

translationNotes.term: The estate goes to the crown
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בֵּית הָמָן (beit Haman, the house of Haman)
translationNotes.note: A condemned man's property was forfeit to the king, which is why 8:1 has Ahasuerus giving the house of Haman to Esther that same day and Mordecai receiving the signet ring taken back from him. The pole he raised, the estate he built, and the ring he sealed the edict with all change hands inside two verses.

stories.keyTakeaway: At Esther’s second banquet she identifies Haman as the enemy; Haman is executed on the pole he had prepared for Mordecai.

stories.title: 🎉 Esther 8
summaryBullets: That same day King Xerxes awarded Queen Esther the estate of Haman, the enemy of the Jews. And Mordecai entered the king’s presence because Esther had revealed his relation to her. (8:1).
The king removed the signet ring he had recovered from Haman and presented it to Mordecai. And Esther appointed Mordecai over the estate of Haman. (8:2).
And once again, Esther addressed the king. She fell at his feet weeping and begged him to revoke the evil scheme of Haman the Agagite, which he had devised against the Jews. (8:3).
The king extended the gold scepter toward Esther, and she arose and stood before the king. (8:4).

“If it pleases the king,” she said, “and if I have found favor in his sight, and the matter seems proper to the king, and I am pleasing in his sight, may an order be written to revoke the letters that the scheming Haman son of Hammedatha, the Agagite, wrote to destroy the Jews in all the king’s provinces. (8:5).
For how could I bear to see the disaster that would befall my people? How could I bear to see the destruction of my kindred?” (8:6).
So King Xerxes said to Esther the Queen and Mordecai the Jew, “Behold, I have given Haman’s estate to Esther, and he was hanged on the gallows because he attacked the Jews. (8:7).

Now you may write in the king’s name as you please regarding the Jews, and seal it with the royal signet ring. For a decree that is written in the name of the king and sealed with the royal signet ring cannot be revoked.” (8:8).

At once the royal scribes were summoned, and on the twenty-third day of the third month (the month of Sivan), they recorded all of Mordecai’s orders to the Jews and to the satraps, governors, and princes of the 127 provinces from India to Cush — writing to each province in its own script, to every people in their own language, and to the Jews in their own script and language. (8:9).
Mordecai wrote in the name of King Xerxes and sealed it with the royal signet ring. He sent the documents by mounted couriers riding on swift horses bred from the royal mares. (8:10).

By these letters the king permitted the Jews in each and every city the right to assemble and defend themselves, to destroy, kill, and annihilate all the forces of any people or province hostile to them, including women and children, and to plunder their possessions. (8:11).
The single day appointed throughout all the provinces of King Xerxes was the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, the month of Adar. (8:12).
A copy of the text of the edict was to be issued in every province and published to all the people, so that the Jews would be ready on that day to avenge themselves on their enemies. (8:13).
The couriers rode out in haste on their royal horses, pressed on by the command of the king. And the edict was also issued in the citadel of Susa. (8:14).
Mordecai went out from the presence of the king in royal garments of blue and white, with a large gold crown and a purple robe of fine linen. And the city of Susa shouted and rejoiced. (8:15).
For the Jews it was a time of light and gladness, of joy and honor. (8:16).

In every province and every city, wherever the king’s edict and decree reached, there was joy and gladness among the Jews, with feasting and celebrating. And many of the people of the land themselves became Jews, because the fear of the Jews had fallen upon them. (8:17).
crossRefs: 1 Kings 21:8-11: Jezebel writes letters in Ahab's name, seals them with his seal, and the elders act on them as law.
Daniel 6:14-17: A decree sealed with the king's signet cannot be changed, and the stone over the den is sealed the same way.
Esther 3:12-15: The first edict, written in every script, sealed with the same ring and sent by the same couriers.
2 Chronicles 30:6-10: Couriers carry the king's letters on foot through all Israel and Judah from town to town.
Ezra 1:1-4: A Persian king puts a decree in writing that reverses the empire's whole policy toward the exiles.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: טַבַּעַת (tabba'at) - Greek: δακτύλιος (daktylios)
translationNotes.note: Persian documents were rolled, tied and sealed with clay or wax stamped by an engraved ring or cylinder. The stamp was the signature: whoever held the ring could commit the crown. Ahasuerus gives it to Haman in 3:10, takes it back at Haman's death, and hands it to Mordecai in 8:2, and each transfer moves the power to make law.

translationNotes.term: Written in the king's name and sealed cannot be revoked
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כְּתָב אֲשֶׁר־נִכְתָּב בְּשֵׁם־הַמֶּלֶךְ (ketav asher nikhtav beshem hammelekh)
translationNotes.note: The rule stated in 8:8 is the hinge of the plot: the first decree cannot be cancelled, only answered. So a second decree is written granting the Jews in every city the right to assemble and defend their lives on the same day (8:11). Daniel 6:8-15 turns on the identical principle, the law of the Medes and Persians that cannot be altered.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הָאֲחַשְׁתְּרָנִים בְּנֵי הָרַמָּכִים (ha-achashteranim benei ha-rammakhim)
translationNotes.note: Both words are Persian, and English versions render them as royal horses bred from the royal stud. Verse 14 says the couriers went out in haste, urged on by the king's command, which is the language of a priority dispatch. The first edict took months of lead time; this one has to reach a hundred and twenty-seven provinces before the same fixed date.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: תְּכֵלֶת וָחוּר (tekhelet va-chur, violet-blue and white) - אַרְגָּמָן (argaman, purple)
translationNotes.note: Mordecai comes out of the king's presence in violet and white with a great crown of gold and a mantle of fine linen and purple (8:15). Those are the same two dyes named among the palace hangings in 1:6, both extracted from murex shellfish at enormous cost. The city of Susa shouted and was glad, says the text, which is the reverse of 3:15, where the same city was thrown into confusion.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מִתְיַהֲדִים (mityahadim)
translationNotes.note: A verb built from the name Judah, and it occurs nowhere else in the Hebrew Bible. Verse 17 says many of the peoples of the land did this because the dread of the Jews had fallen on them. The word describes people publicly identifying themselves with the Jewish community, and the text gives fear as the reason without commenting further.

stories.keyTakeaway: Xerxes gives Haman's estate to Esther and his signet ring to Mordecai; Esther then persuades the king to issue a new decree allowing Jews throughout his provinces to assemble and defend themselves against their enemies on the thirteenth day of Adar. Mordecai sends the edict by fast couriers, and the Jews respond with celebration and feasting.

stories.title: 🎉 Esther 9
summaryBullets: On the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, the month of Adar, the king’s command and edict were to be executed. On this day the enemies of the Jews had hoped to overpower them, but their plan was overturned and the Jews overpowered those who hated them. (9:1).

In each of the provinces of King Xerxes, the Jews assembled in their cities to attack those who sought to harm them. No man could withstand them, because the fear of them had fallen upon all peoples. (9:2).
And all the officials of the provinces, the satraps, the governors, and the king’s administrators helped the Jews, because the fear of Mordecai had fallen upon them. (9:3).
For Mordecai exercised great power in the palace, and his fame spread throughout the provinces as he became more and more powerful. (9:4).
The Jews put all their enemies to the sword, killing and destroying them, and they did as they pleased to those who hated them. (9:5).
In the citadel of Susa, the Jews killed and destroyed five hundred men, (9:6).
including Parshandatha, Dalphon, Aspatha, (9:7).
Poratha, Adalia, Aridatha, (9:8).
Parmashta, Arisai, Aridai, and Vaizatha. (9:9).
They killed these ten sons of Haman son of Hammedatha, the enemy of the Jews, but they did not lay a hand on the plunder. (9:10).
On that day the number of those killed in the citadel of Susa was reported to the king, (9:11).

who said to Queen Esther, “In the citadel of Susa the Jews have killed and destroyed five hundred men, including Haman’s ten sons. What have they done in the rest of the royal provinces? Now what is your petition? It will be given to you. And what further do you request? It will be fulfilled.” (9:12).
Esther replied, “If it pleases the king, may the Jews in Susa also have tomorrow to carry out today’s edict, and may the bodies of Haman’s ten sons be hanged on the gallows.” (9:13).
So the king commanded that this be done. An edict was issued in Susa, and they hanged the ten sons of Haman. (9:14).
On the fourteenth day of the month of Adar, the Jews in Susa came together again and put to death three hundred men there, but they did not lay a hand on the plunder. (9:15).

The rest of the Jews in the royal provinces also assembled to defend themselves and rid themselves of their enemies. They killed 75,000 who hated them, but they did not lay a hand on the plunder. (9:16).
This was done on the thirteenth day of the month of Adar, and on the fourteenth day they rested, making it a day of feasting and joy. (9:17).
The Jews in Susa, however, had assembled on the thirteenth and the fourteenth days of the month. So they rested on the fifteenth day, making it a day of feasting and joy. (9:18).
This is why the rural Jews, who live in the villages, observe the fourteenth day of the month of Adar as a day of joy and feasting. It is a holiday for sending gifts to one another. (9:19).
Mordecai recorded these events and sent letters to all the Jews in all the provinces of King Xerxes, both near and far, (9:20).
to establish among them an annual celebration on the fourteenth and fifteenth days of the month of Adar (9:21).

as the days on which the Jews gained rest from their enemies and the month in which their sorrow turned to joy and their mourning into a holiday. He wrote that these were to be days of feasting and joy, of sending gifts to one another and to the poor. (9:22).
So the Jews agreed to continue the custom they had started, as Mordecai had written to them. (9:23).
For Haman son of Hammedatha, the Agagite, the enemy of all the Jews, had plotted against the Jews to destroy them and had cast the Pur (that is, the lot) to crush and destroy them. (9:24).

But when it came before the king, he commanded by letter that the wicked scheme which Haman had devised against the Jews should come back upon his own head, and that he and his sons should be hanged on the gallows. (9:25).
Therefore these days are called Purim, from the word Pur. Because of all the instructions in this letter, and because of all they had seen and experienced, (9:26).

the Jews bound themselves to establish the custom that they and their descendants and all who join them should not fail to celebrate these two days at the appointed time each and every year, according to their regulation. (9:27).

These days should be remembered and celebrated by every generation, family, province, and city, so that these days of Purim should not fail to be observed among the Jews, nor should the memory of them fade from their descendants. (9:28).
So Queen Esther daughter of Abihail, along with Mordecai the Jew, wrote with full authority to confirm this second letter concerning Purim. (9:29).
And Mordecai sent letters with words of peace and truth to all the Jews in the 127 provinces of the kingdom of Xerxes, (9:30).

in order to confirm these days of Purim at their appointed time, just as Mordecai the Jew and Queen Esther had established them and had committed themselves and their descendants to the times of fasting and lamentation. (9:31).
So Esther’s decree confirmed these regulations about Purim, which were written into the record. (9:32).
crossRefs: 1 Samuel 15:17-23: Saul takes the spoil of Amalek and is told that obedience is better than sacrifice.
Exodus 17:14-16: Write this as a memorial in a book: the LORD will have war with Amalek from generation to generation.
Psalm 124:1-8: If the LORD had not been on our side when men rose against us, they would have swallowed us alive.
Nehemiah 8:10-12: The people are told to eat, drink and send portions to those who have nothing prepared.
Exodus 12:14-17: A day is set as a memorial to be kept as a feast throughout your generations, a lasting ordinance.

translationNotes.term: They laid no hand on the plunder
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: וּבַבִּזָּה לֹא שָׁלְחוּ אֶת־יָדָם (u-vabbizzah lo shalechu et yadam)
translationNotes.note: The book says it three separate times (9:10, 15, 16), which in Hebrew narrative is emphasis by repetition. The edict of 8:11 had explicitly granted them the plunder, so this is a right waived, not a rule obeyed. Saul's failure with the Amalekites was precisely that he kept the spoil (1 Samuel 15:19).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אַרְבָּעָה עָשָׂר וַחֲמִשָּׁה עָשָׂר (arba'ah asar va-chamishshah asar, the fourteenth and the fifteenth)
translationNotes.note: In the provinces the fighting was on the thirteenth of Adar and the fourteenth was the day of rest and feasting; in the walled capital the king granted a second day, so Susa rested on the fifteenth (9:15-18). That is why Purim is still kept on two dates: the fourteenth in ordinary towns and the fifteenth in cities that were walled, which is called Shushan Purim.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: יִתָּלוּ עַל־הָעֵץ (yittalu al ha-ets, let them be hanged on the wood)
translationNotes.note: Verses 7-10 record that Haman's ten sons were killed in the fighting; the request in 9:13 is that their bodies then be fastened on the pole. Exposing a body after death was a public display of the sentence, and Deuteronomy 21:22-23 requires that such a body be taken down the same day. Their names are set out in the Hebrew manuscripts in a single vertical column, one per line.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: פּוּרִים (Purim, lots)
translationNotes.note: The feast takes its name from the pur, the die Haman cast to pick the date (9:24-26). Its rules are set out in 9:22: feasting and gladness, sending portions of food to one another, and gifts to the poor. It is the only festival in the Hebrew Bible not commanded at Sinai; Mordecai and Esther establish it by letter, and 9:27 says the Jews took it on themselves and their descendants.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חֲמִשָּׁה וְשִׁבְעִים אֶלֶף (chamishshah veshiv'im elef)
translationNotes.note: That is the total across all hundred and twenty-seven provinces (9:16), against five hundred killed in the citadel of Susa on the first day and three hundred on the second (9:6, 15). The text presents this as the enemies who had risen to carry out the first edict, and it twice notes that no one could stand against them because the fear of them had fallen on the peoples.

stories.keyTakeaway: The Jews defend themselves against their enemies on the thirteenth of Adar, killing seventy-five thousand across the provinces and five hundred in Susa, including Haman's ten sons; Mordecai then establishes an annual celebration called Purim to commemorate their deliverance.

stories.title: 🎉 Esther 10
summaryBullets: Now King Xerxes imposed tribute throughout the land, even to its farthest shores. (10:1).

And all of Mordecai’s powerful and magnificent accomplishments, together with the full account of the greatness to which the king had raised him, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Media and Persia? (10:2).
For Mordecai the Jew was second only to King Xerxes, preeminent among the Jews and highly favored by his many kinsmen, seeking the good of his people and speaking peace to all his countrymen. (10:3).
crossRefs: 2 Kings 25:27-30: Jehoiachin is brought out of prison in Babylon, given a seat above the other kings, and eats at the king's table.
Daniel 2:48: Daniel is made ruler over the province of Babylon and chief prefect over all its wise men.
Nehemiah 2:1-8: Another Jew at the Persian court, a generation later, uses his access to the king for his people.
Jeremiah 29:4-7: Seek the welfare of the city where I have sent you into exile, and pray to the LORD for it.
1 Chronicles 29:29-30: The acts of a king, first and last, written in the records with all his reign and his might.

translationNotes.term: Tribute on the land and the coastlands
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מַס (mas, levy or forced labour)
translationNotes.note: Mas covers both a tax and a corvee, a levy of compulsory work; Solomon raised one for his building projects (1 Kings 5:13-14). Verse 1 has Ahasuerus laying it on the mainland and on the coastlands, the islands and coasts of the Aegean. It is a single line of imperial routine, and it is what the empire looked like on every ordinary day of this story.

translationNotes.term: The chronicles of the kings of Media and Persia
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: סֵפֶר דִּבְרֵי הַיָּמִים לְמַלְכֵי מָדַי וּפָרָס (sefer divrei hayyamim lemalkhei Madai u-Faras)
translationNotes.note: The same official annals that were read out in 6:1 and saved Mordecai's life. Verse 2 says the full account of Ahasuerus' power and of Mordecai's promotion is written there, referring the reader to a state archive that no longer survives. Kings and Chronicles make the same kind of citation to the annals of Israel and Judah.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מִשְׁנֶה לַמֶּלֶךְ (mishneh lammelekh)
translationNotes.note: The post Haman held in 3:1 and Mordecai holds in 10:3, the vizier's place. Joseph occupies the same rank in Egypt (Genesis 41:40-44) and Daniel is made third in the kingdom of Babylon (Daniel 5:29). Verse 3 defines what he did with it: he sought the good of his people and spoke peace to all his kindred.

translationNotes.term: God is never named in this book
translationNotes.note: The Hebrew text of Esther never uses the name of God, or the word prayer, or the law of Moses, or Jerusalem's temple. The Greek version in the Septuagint contains six additional passages that do, including prayers of Mordecai and Esther, and those additions are why Catholic and Orthodox Bibles carry a longer Esther than Jewish and Protestant Bibles do. What the Hebrew records instead is fasting (4:16), the wording of 4:14, and a chain of events with no coincidences in it.

stories.keyTakeaway: King Xerxes collects tribute across his empire while Mordecai, promoted to second rank, becomes preeminent among the Jews and works for the welfare of his people.

intro:
Esther does not name its author. Jewish tradition (preserved in the Talmud, Baba Bathra 15a) attributes the book to Mordecai or to the Men of the Great Assembly (Knesset Gedolah). The book reached its final form in post-exilic Persia or Judah around 460-440 BC, within a generation of the events themselves. Mordecai was a Jew of the tribe of Benjamin, descended from Kish, whose ancestors had been carried into exile with King Jeconiah of Judah in 597 BC during the second Babylonian deportation. He held an administrative position at the Persian royal court in Susa, the empire's winter capital. He raised his orphaned cousin Hadassah (Hebrew for "myrtle"), better known by her Persian throne name Esther (from Persian stara, "star"). The events of the book are set in Susa during the reign of King Xerxes I (Hebrew: Ahasuerus; reigned 486-465 BC). This places the narrative between the completion of the second temple (516 BC, the closing scene of Ezra 6) and Ezra's return to Jerusalem (458 BC, the opening of Ezra 7). The historical setting is the Achaemenid Empire at its territorial maximum, stretching from the Indus River to the Aegean Sea and from the Caucasus to Cush (upper Nile). Xerxes I led the famous Persian invasion of Greece in 480 BC (the battles of Thermopylae, Salamis, and Plataea) before turning to focus on internal administration; he was assassinated in 465 BC, and his son Artaxerxes I succeeded him. Egypt was a Persian satrapy under the 27th Dynasty, periodically restive against Persian rule.

Esther is the seventeenth book of the Christian Old Testament. In the Hebrew Bible it is one of the Five Megillot (Five Scrolls) within the Ketuvim (Writings), traditionally read aloud in synagogues at the Feast of Purim (the festival the book establishes, observed annually on the 14th and 15th of Adar). The Hebrew title Esther is the protagonist's Persian name; the Hebrew name Hadassah means "myrtle." Esther is the only book of the Hebrew Bible that does not mention God by name, and it is also the only book of the Hebrew Bible not represented among the Dead Sea Scrolls discovered at Qumran (mid-20th century AD).
